question: What are the hormone-producing cell clusters located within the pancreas called?
explanation: The endocrine portion of the pancreas contains groups of cells named the islets of Langerhans, which produce insulin and glucagon. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why does damage to the pancreas often lead to both digestive problems and blood sugar issues?

options.A: Digestive enzymes and hormones are stored inside the exact same cells.
options.B: Insulin is required to activate all major pancreatic digestive enzymes.
options.C: The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine functions in one organ.
options.D: The pancreas shares a direct blood supply with the liver and stomach.

explanation: You've got this! The pancreas is a multitasker. It acts as an exocrine gland to help us digest food, and an endocrine gland to manage our blood sugar. When it gets injured, both jobs take a hit. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h1)

question: What are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Stomach ulcers and low dietary fiber
options.B: Bacterial infection and high salt intake

explanation: Gallstones blocking the bile duct and excessive alcohol consumption account for the vast majority of acute pancreatitis cases. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h2)

question: What main process causes tissue damage inside the pancreas during acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Infection of pancreatic tissue by gut bacteria traveling upward
options.B: Rapid formation of scar tissue blocking the pancreatic duct
options.C: Autodigestion of the pancreas by its own early-activated enzymes
options.D: Complete lack of blood supply caused by sudden heart failure

explanation: Think of it as friendly fire! Digestive enzymes turn on too early while still inside the pancreas, and they accidentally start breaking down the organ's own tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h2)

question: Where is the classic pain of acute pancreatitis felt, and where does it usually spread?

options.A: Chest region radiating to the left arm
options.B: Upper abdomen radiating to the back
options.C: Suprapubic area radiating to the lower back
options.D: Lower right abdomen radiating to the thigh

explanation: Spot on! Pancreatic pain is notorious for being felt right in the upper belly and boring straight through to the back. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h3)

question: A patient asks why their belly pain gets worse after eating a meal. What is the best way to explain this?

options.A: Food stretches the stomach wall, putting physical pressure on the pancreas.
options.B: Eating triggers the pancreas to release enzymes, which irritates the inflamed tissue.
options.C: Eating causes bile to back up instantly into the liver, stopping digestion.
options.D: Food particles enter the pancreatic duct directly, blocking the flow of blood.

explanation: Makes sense, right? When food enters the gut, your body tells the pancreas to pump out digestive enzymes. If the pancreas is already inflamed, sending out those juices just makes it hurt more. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h3)

question: What term describes the fatty, foul-smelling stools seen in patients with chronic pancreatitis?
explanation: Great recall! Steatorrhea is the medical term for fatty, oily stools. It happens because the damaged pancreas can't make the enzymes needed to digest fats properly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why do patients with long-standing chronic pancreatitis eventually develop diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Dietary restrictions force the body to rely entirely on stored body fat.
options.B: Scar tissue gradually destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas.
options.C: The liver stops responding to insulin because it is overworked by fat digestion.
options.D: Chronic vomiting causes a permanent chemical imbalance in blood sugar.

explanation: You're doing great! As chronic inflammation forms scar tissue over time, it slowly wipes out the insulin-making cells in the islets of Langerhans, leading to diabetes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which blood test is more specific for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
explanation: Spot on! Serum lipase is the go-to test because it's much more specific to the pancreas than amylase, and it stays elevated longer during an attack. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which imaging test is generally considered the best for viewing tissue death and fluid collections in acute pancreatitis?
explanation: You got it! A contrast CT gives doctors the clearest pictures to spot inflammation, dead tissue, and hidden pockets of fluid around the pancreas. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the main reason a patient with acute pancreatitis is kept NPO (nothing by mouth)?

options.A: To rest the pancreas and stop the release of digestive enzymes
options.B: To prevent choking during sudden episodes of severe vomiting
options.C: To keep the bowel completely clean for diagnostic X-rays
options.D: To prepare the stomach for emergency surgical removal

explanation: Brilliant! Keeping the patient NPO means no food enters the gut, which gives the hardworking pancreas a well-deserved break so it stops producing damaging enzymes. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: When should a patient with chronic pancreatitis take their prescribed pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy?

options.B: Only when eating foods high in sugar

explanation: Spot on! Enzymes need to be taken right along with all food and snacks so they can mix with the nutrients and help the body digest food properly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: What early symptom is typically caused by a tumor in the head of the pancreas blocking the bile duct?
explanation: You're crushing it! When a tumor blocks the bile duct, bilirubin backs up into the bloodstream, turning the skin and eyes yellow (jaundice). [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What complex surgery involves removing the head of the pancreas, the duodenum, and the gallbladder?
explanation: The Whipple procedure is a major operation performed to treat tumors located in the head of the pancreas. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is a major worry when pancreatic fluid leaks from the surgical site after a Whipple procedure?
explanation: Good to know! A leak at the surgical join creates a pancreatic fistula, which can spill harsh digestive juices into the belly and cause a severe infection. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)

question: Which nursing action is MOST important when caring for a patient with active surgical drains after pancreatic surgery?

options.A: Flush the drainage tubing with sterile water every two hours.
options.B: Monitor and record the amount and color of drainage regularly.
options.C: Clamp all surgical drains shut to prevent accidental fluid loss.
options.D: Change the surrounding skin dressings once every week.

explanation: Keep up the great clinical thinking! Tracking your drain output closely helps you catch dangerous warning signs like bleeding or fistulas early. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)
